title: Characteristics Associated with In-Hospital Rebleeding After Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding in a Surgical Cohort in Astana Kazakhstan
content: Background: Rebleeding after initial control of upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB) is clinically important, but institutional data require reproducible case definitions and separation of persistent bleeding from recurrence. We examined characteristics associated with in-hospital rebleeding in an adult surgical cohort in Astana, Kazakhstan. Methods: We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of surgical admissions during 2021-2025. Of 756 initially identified hospitalization episodes, 63 with incomplete or unverifiable required information were excluded. The complete-record dataset contained 693 episodes, including 674 instrumentally confirmed and 19 probable upper sources. The primary analysis included 658 confirmed episodes with initial bleeding control. A five-covariate exploratory logistic model evaluated age, admission hemoglobin, systolic blood pressure, variceal etiology, and active bleeding at first endoscopy. Follow-up ended at discharge, transfer, or in-hospital death. Results: Rebleeding occurred in 42/658 episodes (6.38%; Wilson 95% CI 4.76-8.52). Median admission systolic blood pressure was 99.0 mmHg in episodes with rebleeding and 119.0 mmHg in those without it. Higher systolic blood pressure was associated with lower adjusted odds of rebleeding (odds ratio per 10 mmHg, 0.83; 95% CI 0.70-0.97). Estimates for age, hemoglobin, variceal etiology, and active bleeding were imprecise and their confidence intervals included unity. Within the confirmed-source cohort, persistent bleeding occurred in 16/674 episodes (2.37%) and in-hospital death in 17/674 (2.52%). Conclusion: Lower admission systolic blood pressure was associated with in-hospital rebleeding after initial control in this selected surgical cohort. The small number of events, complete-record selection, and absence of linked post-discharge follow-up limit interpretation. These exploratory findings require confirmation and do not constitute a validated prediction model.
